failures.rule: the spec's worked example: array concatenation with a substitution is a common way to add to paths
the spec's worked example: a later array definition can concatenate a substitution referring to its own earlier value with a new array

${a} in a's own value refers to the earlier a, an object, so the concatenation merges {p: ...} with {q: 1}; the inner p is itself a merge of an object and a substitution. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) when the merge inside a concatenation piece resolves, as in 018

the null at r only stops merging at r; ${r} is the object {x:1}, and a later object merges with the earlier a, so helper stays. typesafe/config carries r's null through the substitution and drops helper (lightbend/config#864)
the same rule one level down: the null in v.nested's history belongs to v.nested, so a.nested still merges with the substituted {x:1} (lightbend/config#864)

a substitution sees the resolved value of the field it names, so o24bbd equals a.nested, which keeps helper. The key name is chosen to sort before a in typesafe/config's root HashMap, the order in which the first version of lightbend/config#864 answered differently for the two
the null belongs to v's history even when v's object is still unresolved, so a merges and keeps helper (lightbend/config#864)

${r} is an object, so it merges with the earlier a and the ${missing} inside it is evaluated: an error. typesafe/config 1.4.5 agreed; 1.4.9 drops the earlier a and yields {y:1}, and lightbend/config#864 restores the error

v's value is a merge whose top is an object and whose null sits further down, under nested; that null is still v.nested's merge instruction, so a.nested keeps helper (lightbend/config#864 review, round 3)
four values for a, two of them substitutions that resolve to objects: all four merge in order
the object layer of a's merge contains a field b that is itself a merge of a substitution and an object; both levels merge
the included file leaves a as an object merged with a substitution; that whole stack merges with the object the including file set earlier
the earlier value is itself a substitution; once everything resolves to objects, all three layers merge
the earlier value is a number, so the included object stack replaces it and merges only within itself
the same as 013 with the included stack the other way up, an object over a substitution; the result does not depend on which layer is on top

an included file may intend to refer to the application's root config, for example to get a value from the environment; the original path CONFORMANCE_HOME is looked up and falls back to the environment variable
an undefined optional that would override keeps the previous value, so common.x.y is 9 and found at the fixed-up path; the original path is not consulted
an object merged with a substitution in the included file keeps working after the fix-up, whichever of the two is on top: q is found at p.q
the string inside url() is interpreted as a URL, and x.conf has no scheme, so it is not one
failures.open_question: the spec says only that the string inside url() is interpreted as a URL; it does not say whether a string that is not a URL is an error or an unresolvable, hence ignorable, resource. typesafe/config rejects it

failures.rule: the separator may be omitted before {, and the spec does not say whether a newline may stand between the key and the brace; typesafe/config and pyhocon accept it, hocon-rs rejects it
failures.open_question: the spec is silent on a newline between a key and its brace; implementations disagree

failures.rule: the [] suffix collects CONFORMANCE_LIST_0, CONFORMANCE_LIST_1, ... until an index is missing, into a list of strings
with no CONFORMANCE_LIST_0 set, an optional ${?X[]} is undefined and the field is not created
indices are collected from 0 until one is missing, so with _0 and _2 set the list holds only the first
an element taken from the environment is a string, so 1 stays "1"
the [] suffix collects environment variables only, so the config key a_0 is not gathered and the optional substitution is undefined
the conversion should be done in a concatenation when a list is expected and an object with numeric keys is found, so the trailing object concatenates onto the array as elements x, y
the conversion should ignore any keys which do not parse as positive integers, so key "foo" is dropped and only "0" contributes to the resulting array

the conversion should sort by the integer value of each key and then build the array; missing indices such as "1" are eliminated rather than left as gaps, so keys "0" and "2" become a two-element array
the conversion ignores any keys which do not parse as positive integers, and "-1" is not a positive integer, so it is dropped and only key "0" contributes
a += b transforms into a = ${?a} [b], and because the fallback is optional (${?a} not ${a}) this is legal even as the first mention of a in the file
+= appends an element to a previous array
each += appends to the value the previous line left, so two of them append two elements
inside an object, += desugars to a self-reference by the field's full path o.a; the appended element may itself be a substitution
b has no previous value, so b += 1 is b = ${?b} [1] with the optional part undefined: [1]. typesafe/config refuses += inside a list because its desugared path cannot name a list element
the self-reference += desugars to uses the full path of the field, o.p.a, even when the enclosing key was written as the path o.p

l += v is l = ${?l} [v]; the appended object holds a merge of an object and a substitution, which resolves inside the new list. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) for the same reason as array-and-object-concatenation/018
when foo:${foo} is merged with an earlier value for foo, the self-reference resolves to that overridden value, so foo ends up { a : 1 }

if the self-referential foo:${foo} comes before foo has any value, the reference is undefined, exactly as if it named a path not found in the document, so it is an error even though foo is given a value afterward
because the self-reference error is treated as undefined rather than an intractable cycle, the optional syntax foo:${?foo} makes the field disappear silently instead of erroring
a self-reference resolves to the value below it even as part of a path expression, so ${foo.a} refers to { c : 1 } rather than 2, and the final merge is { a : 2, c : 1 }
an optional self-reference in a value concatenation has to look back to an undefined a, so a ends up "foo" rather than "foofoo"

this case has undefined behavior depending on resolution order: implementations are allowed to set both a and b to 1, both to 2, or to error, but must set both to the same value because substitutions are memoized by instance, so a and b must never diverge (e.g. a=1,b=2 is not permitted)
failures.open_question: the spec allows both fields to be 1, both 2, or an error (L875-877); only 'the same value' is required, which one expected tree cannot express. typesafe/config itself gives 1 or 2 depending on key order

failures.rule: a substituted object merges with the earlier object, so its fields are part of the result and ${does-not-exist} is an error
an undefined optional that would override leaves the previous value in place, so the list is the result and ${does-not-exist} is evaluated: an error
a genuine cycle is an error for required substitutions; with the optional syntax it is a missing value, so neither field is created
the text ${a} appears twice and resolves differently: to x in a's own self-reference and to the final xy in b; memoizing by path instead of by instance would give b the wrong value
a field may look up its own older value before being overridden with a new value based on it, letting path:${path}":d" extend the earlier path:"a:b:c"
a value concatenation containing a substitution to its own field is self-referential, so ${a} looks back to the earlier x and the result is xbc
the spec lists path:${path} [ /usr/bin ] among the examples of self-referential fields: a value concatenation of a substitution with an array literal is still self-referential
a substitution whose path is not defined in the configuration falls back to an environment variable of the same name
a required ${x} substitution that is not present in the configuration tree is searched for in the environment and resolves to the variable's value instead of being an error
the lookup is case-sensitive all the way until the env variable fallback is reached, so a lowercase key does not shadow an uppercase substitution and the environment variable is used
an env variable set to the empty string is kept as such, so a required substitution resolves to "" rather than being undefined
an env variable set to the empty string is set to empty string rather than undefined, so an optional ${?x} substitution creates the field with "" instead of dropping it
environment variables always become a string value, so values that would parse as a number, a boolean or null in HOCON stay the strings "42", "true" and "null"
if an undefined ${?foo} would override a previously-set value for the same field, the previous value remains
quoted strings are JSON strings, and JSON's grammar accepts any \uXXXX escape, an unpaired surrogate included, so the string holds that one code unit
